enrichment.short_title: Tripartite settlement agreement void for uncertainty where $100m sum was conditional on FGN conduct
key_facts: Noga, the Federal Government of Nigeria (FGN), and the SJ Berwin defendants disputed whether three August 1999 agreements settled complex litigation over Ajaokuta bills and related claims.
The tripartite agreement of 11 August 1999 referred to 'a settlement sum' without stating $100 million; Noga sought to supply that figure by parol evidence.
Rix LJ found $100 million had been agreed orally between Noga and the SJ Berwin defendants only on condition that FGN took nothing more for Ajaokuta and did not breach that understanding.
The 13 August agreement was superseded by a 16 August agreement under which FGN waived only Ajaokuta claims in return for DM 300 million.
The SJ Berwin defendants appealed on bindingness of the tripartite agreement and on whether there was consideration for the 16 August agreement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: First-stage appeal to the Court of Appeal on preliminary settlement-agreement issues following a six-month trial before Rix LJ, with further appeal points reserved.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed on both issues heard: tripartite agreement not binding (majority); consideration found for the 16 August agreement.
enrichment.ratio: Where parol evidence is needed to identify an uncertain contractual term, the court must ask whether the parties objectively intended that term to be inserted so as to produce a final binding contract at signing; conditional prior negotiations can show the document was not intended to be final and binding, and rescission and replacement of an executory contract can supply fresh consideration even if rescission and replacement occur simultaneously.
legal_issues: Whether parol evidence could identify 'a settlement sum' as $100 million so as to make the tripartite agreement binding
Whether conditionality in pre-signature negotiations meant no final binding agreement was made
Whether the 16 August agreement lacked consideration because it merely varied the 13 August agreement

enrichment.short_title: Unfair dismissal time limit cannot be resolved at preliminary hearing without full evidence on constructive dismissal
key_facts: Mr Donlon, an area housing manager, was dismissed in 2000 but reinstated on appeal with a final written warning; his employers then refused to return him to his substantive post.
On 18 October 2000 management proposed redeployment rather than reinstatement to his former role; Mr Donlon remained on sick leave and payroll.
On 2 March 2001 the chief officer confirmed he would not return as area housing manager; Mr Donlon treated this as the effective dismissal date.
The employment tribunal at a preliminary hearing held dismissal occurred on 18 October 2000 and that his claim was out of time.
The Employment Appeal Tribunal set aside the dismissal finding and remitted the case for a substantive hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer's appeal to the Court of Appeal against the Employment Appeal Tribunal's decision remitting the unfair dismissal claim for rehearing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; matter remitted for full hearing on whether and when dismissal occurred and whether it was unfair.
enrichment.ratio: Whether an employee was dismissed, and if so when, for limitation purposes under the Employment Rights Act 1996 cannot safely be determined at a preliminary hearing on incomplete evidence where constructive dismissal is in issue; repudiatory conduct requires acceptance and managerial officers may lack authority to override an appeal board reinstatement.
legal_issues: Whether there was a dismissal at all
When the effective date of termination occurred for section 111 purposes
Whether repudiation and acceptance principles applied to events in October 2000 or March 2001
Whether the preliminary hearing was an appropriate shortcut

enrichment.short_title: Similar-fact evidence from earlier South Wales police investigations admissible in malicious prosecution claim
key_facts: Michael O'Brien claimed damages for malicious prosecution and misfeasance arising from the police investigation that led to his murder conviction, quashed in 2000 after more than eleven years in custody.
He sought to rely on similar-fact evidence from the Welsh bomb trial (R v Griffiths) and the Idris Ali murder investigation, both involving DI Lewis and DCS Carsley.

A High Court judge at a case management conference permitted limited similar-fact evidence relating to alleged fabrication of cell confessions, oppressive interviewing, denial of solicitors, and related misconduct.
The Chief Constable appealed against admission of Griffiths evidence; O'Brien cross-appealed on exclusion of evidence about a sex-offender cellmate informer.
The Court of Appeal reviewed civil similar-fact law under CPR 32.1 and DPP v P.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory appeal and cross-appeal on admissibility and discretionary exclusion of similar-fact evidence before trial of a civil claim against the police.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; limited Griffiths and Ali similar-fact evidence remains admissible; cross-appeal allowed on sex-offender cellmate evidence.
enrichment.ratio: In civil proceedings similar-fact evidence is admissible if logically probative of an issue in the case; once admissible, CPR 32.1(2) permits exclusion only where trial manageability, cost, complexity, or unfairness outweigh probative force, but exceptionally serious alleged investigative malpractice by the same officers may justify admission despite lengthening the trial.
legal_issues: Whether civil similar-fact evidence must show striking similarity or system of conduct
Application of DPP v P admissibility test in civil cases
Exercise of discretion under CPR 32.1(2) where trial may be extended by weeks
Whether R v Edwards credit-control principles applied in civil discovery context

enrichment.short_title: Solicitor liable for loss of chance where late RTA insurer notice destroyed viable pedestrian injury claim
key_facts: Micah Sharpe suffered serious head injuries when struck by a taxi while crossing a road at night after passengers disembarked from a bus.
Solicitor Michael Addison issued proceedings against the driver but gave insurers notice under section 152 one day late, destroying RTA indemnity.
Counsel and legal aid authorities had previously advised the claim had real merit despite high contributory negligence.
The underlying action was discontinued; Sharpe sued Addison for losing the chance to recover damages from the driver.
The trial judge held the underlying claim worthless and awarded nothing; he also undervalued lost earnings.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against dismissal of a secondary claim for solicitors' negligence following discontinuance of the primary PI action.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; underlying claim had more than negligible value and overall recovery assessed at about 10% of full quantum, yielding an award of over £50,000.
enrichment.ratio: In solicitors' negligence the claimant must show the lost litigation had real and substantial prospects, with a heavy evidential burden on the solicitor where he previously advised pursuit; once that hurdle is cleared, prospects are evaluated generously and overlapping liability/contributory negligence discounts must not double-count the same causation factors.
legal_issues: Whether the underlying PI claim was worthless or had real prospects
Evidential burden where solicitor had advised the claim was viable
Valuation of lost chance after inevitable 75% contributory negligence
Whether lost earnings should be assessed by multiplicand/multiplier rather than low lump sum

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review refused over City Academy outline permission on Paterson Park open space

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Environmental Impact Assessment) (England and Wales) Regulations 1999

key_facts: Southwark Council resolved in January 2002 to grant outline planning permission for a 1,200-pupil City Academy on Paterson Park in Bermondsey, conflicting with UDP open-space protection policies.
The Mayor initially directed refusal for unacceptable open-space loss but withdrew the direction after compensatory open-space and community-use undertakings in 2002.
Outline permission was issued on 14 November 2002 following a section 106 agreement; a separate temporary school application followed.

Resident claimant Mrs Lambert challenged the lawfulness of the process, including officer report fairness, post-resolution material considerations, conformity of the permission notice, and EIA screening.
The council had screened the project in September 2001 and concluded no environmental statement was required.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of planning decisions after permission granted on 7 April 2003; permission to appeal refused at hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed on all four grounds; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A planning officer's report need not be perfect if it fairly presents material considerations under sections 54A and 70; post-committee steps securing mayoral approval and section 106 obligations did not require fresh committee reconsideration where they did not alter the outline permission granted; a secondary school on previously developed urban land exceeding 0.5 hectares was not irrational EIA development, and a later temporary school application did not transform the project into EIA development.

Whether new matters between January and November 2002 required committee reconsideration under section 70(2)
Whether the November 2002 permission notice conformed to earlier resolutions
Whether EIA screening was flawed or should have been revised

enrichment.short_title: Relief from sanction refused where appellant repeatedly breached unless orders on security for costs
key_facts: Contract Facilities Ltd sued shareholders for breach of a share purchase agreement to buy Glaslyn Retirement Homes; the company had been struck off before completion and was later restored.
HHJ Weeks held Contract Facilities was not ready, willing and able to complete, the contract was lawfully terminated, and restoration did not revive it.
The appeal was conditional on security for costs; Contract Facilities failed to comply with unless orders, paying cheques late or with only one signature.
Waller LJ had previously granted relief by a narrow margin after a 12-minute late payment but warned further breaches would not be tolerated.
On the hearing date the £37,000 court cheque had not cleared and the £11,791 cheque to respondents' solicitors bounced.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for relief from sanction under CPR 3.9 after the appeal was struck out for non-compliance with a unless order made four days before the listed appeal hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Relief from sanction refused; appeal dismissed with costs and funds in court ordered paid out to respondents.
enrichment.ratio: Relief from sanction under CPR 3.9 requires fresh consideration of all circumstances, but repeated deliberate or reckless non-compliance with unless orders, especially after clear warnings and a pattern of stalling costs enforcement, will ordinarily justify refusing relief even where non-compliance is partly explained as administrative error.
legal_issues: Whether failure to comply with the unless order of 11 July 2003 was intentional or excusable
Whether the court should grant relief where substantial costs had already been incurred on the appeal
Effect of prior history of late payment and costs stalling on CPR 3.9(1)(e)

enrichment.short_title: Extradition habeas corpus granted where Czech Republic failed to prove applicant unlawfully at large
key_facts: Julie Ginova, a Czech national, was convicted of robbery in 1994 and sentenced to two years' imprisonment.
Her sentence was repeatedly suspended for pregnancy-related reasons, most recently until 17 May 1999; she did not surrender to custody thereafter.
On 27 May 1999 she applied for a further suspension but left for the United Kingdom before any substantive decision; extradition was later sought.
A district judge held she appeared to be unlawfully at large; Ginova applied for habeas corpus challenging the sufficiency of Czech law evidence.
The Czech presiding judge's statement focused on limitation and did not clearly establish that Ginova was arrestable without further judicial process after 27 May 1999.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Habeas corpus application following extradition committal proceedings under the Extradition Act 1989.
enrichment.outcome: Application allowed; applicant discharged from custody; costs awarded to applicant including LSC assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 9(8)(b) of the Extradition Act 1989 the requesting state must prove to the criminal standard that the person appears to be unlawfully at large, meaning liable to arrest without further court order; gaps in foreign-law evidence and unexplained periods when the applicant remained at liberty after suspension expiry can prevent that burden being discharged even where suspension orders suggest automatic reactivation of sentence.
legal_issues: Whether Ginova became unlawfully at large on expiry of suspension on 17 May 1999
Whether Czech law required further procedural steps before arrest after suspension ended
Standard and burden of proof on the requesting state
Admissibility and sufficiency of foreign judicial statements

enrichment.short_title: Gearbox warranty limitation split as replacement-supply and guarantee claims survive strike-out
area_of_law: Sale of goods and supply of services
key_facts: VAI Industries (successor to Davy McKee) bought gearbox equipment from Bostock for Hindalco aluminium rolling mill modifications in India under a September 1994 purchase order.
The order contained a 24-month warranty from FOB delivery and standard terms including a three-year latent-defect guarantee from acceptance.
Equipment was delivered FOB on 28 July 1995; provisional acceptance occurred around March 1997; the main drive gearbox failed catastrophically in August 1998.
David Brown supplied replacement parts in 1999 after disputes, but failures continued and a redesigned unit was ordered from Italy in 2001.
Curtis J struck out the claim as statute-barred, treating the cause of action as arising at delivery in July 1995.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission treated as preliminary issue on limitation, following strike-out/summary judgment application under CPR 3.4 and 24.2.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: majority held warranty claim not statute-barred; guarantee and replacement-contract claims restored for trial; Carnwath LJ dissenting on warranty.
enrichment.ratio: A contractual warranty that equipment remain free from design defects for up to 24 months from FOB can impose a continuing obligation breachable on each day within that period, so limitation runs from the last day of the warranty rather than delivery; separately, a guarantee requiring latent defects appearing within three years of acceptance to be made good gives a fresh cause of action when replacement parts are supplied, and a November 1998 agreement to replace defective parts may found a distinct contract.
legal_issues: Whether the 24-month warranty created a continuing obligation or only assessed quality at delivery
Whether clause 8 guarantee survived alongside the purchase-order warranty
When acceptance occurred for the three-year guarantee period
Whether 1999 replacement work created a new contract not barred by limitation

enrichment.short_title: Millennium Dome liquidation upheld after register rectification and valid solvency declaration
key_facts: NMEC, the public body that operated the Millennium Dome, was placed into members' voluntary liquidation in December 2001 by Lord Falconer as sole shareholder.
GMEL claimed up to £1.6 billion damages arising from trademark disputes and alleged conspiracy to ruin its Greenwich millennium exhibition business.
Lord Falconer had not been entered on the register of members due to an administrative error; Lightman J retrospectively rectified the register in April 2002 without notice to GMEL.

GMEL challenged the rectification and argued NMEC's section 89 declaration of solvency was invalid because the attached statement of assets and liabilities omitted Dome proceeds, undrawn grant, and provisions.
KPMG liquidators rejected GMEL's proof of debt except for £3,520 costs and sought declarations validating the liquidation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Companies Court applications by GMEL to set aside rectification and challenge the nature of NMEC's voluntary liquidation, opposed by former shareholders and liquidators.
enrichment.outcome: GMEL's applications dismissed; declarations made that NMEC has been in members' voluntary winding up since 18 December 2001 and liquidators validly appointed.
enrichment.ratio: A creditor without a legitimate interest in membership rectification lacks standing to set aside an order under section 359 correcting an obvious register error where shares are fully paid and public documents already showed the true member; minor or debatable errors in a section 89 statement of assets and liabilities do not deprive it of status as such a statement under De Courcy v Clements, so a declaration of solvency remains effective.
legal_issues: Whether GMEL had standing to challenge retrospective rectification of the register of members
Whether deficiencies in the section 89 statement invalidated the declaration of solvency
Whether NMEC's interest in Dome sale proceeds and undrawn lottery grant should have been included as assets
Whether liquidation deprived GMEL of legitimate disclosure rights

enrichment.short_title: Costs of security-for-costs application in Noga litigation remain payable in any event
key_facts: In the Noga commercial litigation, Rix J on 30 July 1999 discharged £180,000 of a £325,000 bank guarantee on condition Noga undertook to provide that sum as security for costs if required.
On 4 November 1999 Longmore J ordered Noga to provide £180,000 security for costs and ordered Noga to pay the SJ Berwin defendants' costs of that application in any event.
Rix LJ later rectified his July order to add the words 'by the court' to the undertaking and granted late permission to appeal the November costs order.
Noga sought to set aside Longmore J's costs order and recover 50% indemnity costs, relying on subsequent trial findings adverse to the SJ Berwin defendants.
The Court of Appeal heard the appeal years after the interlocutory order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Late appeal against an interlocutory costs order made during security-for-costs applications in the Noga proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Longmore J's order that Noga pay the security application costs in any event stands.
enrichment.ratio: An interlocutory order for costs in any event must be judged by the circumstances when it was made, not by later trial outcomes; even if a judge misunderstood an earlier undertaking, that does not necessarily justify revisiting the costs order years later absent exceptional circumstances.
legal_issues: Whether Longmore J's costs order was based on a misapprehension of Rix J's undertaking
Whether subsequent trial findings of dishonesty against the SJ Berwin defendants should affect an earlier interlocutory costs order
Whether the appeal should be entertained given the delay
